Shows the trade-off between spending today and security tomorrow.

faqs.a: Withdraw 4% of your portfolio in year one, then adjust for inflation yearly. Historically this lasted 30 years for a 50/50 stock-bond mix. It is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee - many planners now suggest 3.5-4%.
Spend less, earn more return (with more risk), delay retirement to save longer, or add income (part-time work, rental). Cutting spending 10% often adds more years than chasing 1% extra return.
faqs.q: How can I make my money last longer?

faqs.a: Yes. At 3% inflation, $40,000 of spending becomes $72,000 in 20 years. Money that ignores inflation runs out years earlier than a no-inflation scenario.
faqs.q: Does inflation really matter that much?

faqs.a: Then you are spending principal. That is normal in retirement - the question is only whether the principal lasts as long as you need. This calculator answers exactly that.
faqs.q: What if my withdrawal exceeds my return?

faqs.a: When your yearly withdrawal is smaller than what your savings earn (after inflation), the balance grows forever on paper. Real markets still vary, so treat it as comfortable, not certain.
No. The simulation runs entirely in your browser.

how-long-will-my-money-last-calculator.formula:
Each year: balance = balance x (1 + r) - withdrawal; withdrawal grows by inflation i.
Closed form (no inflation): n = -ln(1 - P x r / W) / ln(1 + r)
P = savings, r = return, W = yearly withdrawal. Simulated year-by-year here.
howTo: Enter your current savings or retirement nest egg.
Set a realistic expected annual return after fees (4-6% is common for balanced portfolios).
Enter what you plan to spend per year.
Add expected inflation for spending growth.
Read how many years your money lasts - and what you would withdraw in total.
keyFacts: Money lasts n years where n is about -ln(1 - savings x r / withdrawal) / ln(1 + r).
Withdrawals above the annual return eat principal - and shrinking principal earns less each year.
Inflation is the silent killer: 3% inflation doubles your spending need every 24 years.
The famous 4% rule: withdrawing 4% yearly (adjusted for inflation) historically lasted 30 years.
Sequence risk: bad returns in the first years of retirement hurt far more than bad returns later.
Cutting spending 10% can add years to your money - small leaks sink the longest retirements.

how-long-will-my-money-last-calculator.workedExample:
$500,000 savings, 5% return, $40,000/year, 0% inflation:
1. Year 1: 500,000 x 1.05 - 40,000 = $485,000
2. Repeating yearly, the balance hits zero during year 21.
3. Money lasts about 20 full years.
4. Total withdrawn is about 20 x $40,000 = $800,000 - far more than the $500,000 saved, thanks to growth.
